newsitem.title: ESTONIA: ESTONIA - MAY SEEK CREDIT RATING LATE '97-PM ADVISER.
newsitem.headline: ESTONIA - MAY SEEK CREDIT RATING LATE '97-PM ADVISER.

text.p: Estonia may seek a country credit rating later this year with opposition to such a move waning, the prime minister's economic adviser and central bank board member Ardo Hansson said on Monday.

Hansson said the Estonian Banking Association and the central bank had met recently to discuss the possibility of seeking a credit rating and would meet again in the next month or two to continue discussions.
"We could do it later this year if the banks want to put up the cash for it," Hansson told Reuters.
"There is less resistance now than a while back because of the fact that the rating may not be as good as it would have been before."

Hansson said Estonia, the only one of the three Baltic countries not to yet have an international credit rating, had previously resisted seeking a rating, thinking it would bring further foreign capital into Estonia. "There is so much money
flowing in already that we didn't want to add fuel to the fire," he said.
"The disadvantage of being small iS that you are so much more sensitive to the inward and outwards flows.
"Excessive optimism about the Estonian economy is one of the most serious problems we are facing."
However with the country's current account deficit now seen as cooling down the small Baltic state's economy, Hansson said opposition to a credit rating was subsiding. "With the
balance of payments situation I don't think Estonia would get as good a credit rating as it would have six months ago, and I would be surprised if got a better credit rating that Latvia," he said.

He said to date the government, with a balanced budget, had not had any need to borrow funds on the international stage. For backing it had gone through the World Bank or Europan Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD). Hansson said the
commercial banks in Estonia already had easy access to foreign funds.
"But the banks say they want cheaper and longterm money and the credit ratings would open this up," Hansson said. "It is not a question of quantity but price."
-- Belinda Goldsmith, Tallinn newsroom +372 630 8400 or reuters@reuters.ee
